title: CSC3710 - Sept 22, 2026: Regular expressions, identities, and intro to DFAs

questions.q: Which regular expression describes exactly the strings over {a, b} of length less than 3?
questions.explain: List each allowed length: λ (length 0), a ∪ b (length 1), (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b) (length 2). Leaving out λ misses the empty string. The third choice is exactly length 3, and the last is length 2 or more.

questions.q: Which regular expression describes the strings over {a, b} of length greater than 3, that is, length at least 4?
questions.explain: Four required symbols followed by (a ∪ b)* for anything extra. The first choice only forces 3 symbols, the second is exactly length 4, and the last allows any length, including λ.

questions.q: Which regular expressions describe the strings over {a, b} that contain the substring ab AND have length greater than 2?
choices: (a ∪ b)*ab(a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)* ∪ (a ∪ b)*(a ∪ b)ab(a ∪ b)*
questions.explain: ab needs at least one more symbol either before it or after it. The four-case version (aab, bab, aba, abb with anything around them) and the two-case version (a symbol follows ab, or a symbol precedes ab) are both correct, which shows that one set can have many regular expressions. (a ∪ b)*ab(a ∪ b)* wrongly includes ab itself (length 2). The last choice misses strings like aab and bab, where ab is at the end.

questions.q: Strings over {a, b} of length 2 or more in which all a's come before all b's. Which regular expressions describe this set? (Here x⁺ means xx*, one or more.)
questions.explain: a⁺b⁺ misses all-a and all-b strings such as aa and bbb, so they are added with aaa* and bbb*, which keep the length at least 2. aaa*b* ∪ aa*bb* ∪ bbb* is another correct form: 2+ a's then any b's, or 1+ a's then 1+ b's, or 2+ b's. a*b* wrongly includes λ, a, and b. a⁺b⁺ ∪ a⁺ ∪ b⁺ wrongly includes a and b, which are too short.

questions.q: Regular expressions over an alphabet are built from the alphabet symbols (plus λ and ∅) using parentheses and which operations only?
questions.explain: In class: use the alphabet symbols and form expressions with union, Kleene star, and concatenation. That's it. No other operations are allowed.

questions.q: (((a ∪ bbb)*bb)* ∪ bab)* is a valid regular expression over {a, b}.
questions.explain: This was the in-class example. It uses only alphabet symbols, union, concatenation, Kleene star, and parentheses, so it is a regular expression no matter how deeply it is nested.

questions.q: Each regular set has exactly one correct regular expression, so if your answer looks different from the key, it must be wrong.
questions.explain: The same set can have many correct regular expressions. For example, the four-case and two-case expressions for 'contains ab, length > 2' are equal. Check equivalence with the online tool instead of comparing by eye.

questions.q: Regular expressions are abbreviated notation for regular sets. Which set does the regular expression (a ∪ ab)* denote?
questions.explain: Union inside the star gives the set {a, ab}, and the star allows any concatenation of those building blocks, including λ. {a}*{ab}* would force every a before every ab, and {a, b}* allows strings like bb that (a ∪ ab)* cannot produce.

questions.q: Choose the regular set(s) over {a, b} to which the string abba belongs.
questions.explain: (a ∪ ab)*ba: take ab from the starred part, then ba. (a ∪ b)*bb(a ∪ b)*: a · bb · a. Not in (a ∪ ab)*: every b comes right after an a, so bb is impossible. Not in (a ∪ b)*ab: every string ends with b, but abba ends with a. Not in the finite set: every string there has length 5, and abba has length 4.

questions.q: What is the quickest justification that abba is NOT in the set described by (a ∪ b)*ab?
choices: Every string in the set has even length
Every string in the set ends with b, but abba ends with a
Every string in the set starts with a, but abba starts with b
The set is finite and abba is not listed
questions.explain: In class: strings in this set 'for sure end with b', so abba is ruled out immediately. Looking for a property that every string in the set has (last symbol, length, building blocks) is the standard way to show a string is NOT in a set.

questions.q: Why can't abba be built from the building blocks of (a ∪ ab)*?
choices: Every string in the set has odd length
The set is finite, and abba is not one of its elements
Every b produced by these blocks comes right after an a, so bb can never appear
Every string in the set must start with ab
questions.explain: The only blocks are a and ab. Each b comes inside an ab block, so it always follows an a, and abba's bb can't be formed. The set is infinite, it contains even-length strings like aa, and it contains strings that start with a alone, such as a.

questions.q: aab is in the set described by (a ∪ ab)*.
questions.explain: Cut it into building blocks: a · ab. Each piece is in {a, ab}, so the string is in {a, ab}*.

questions.q: abba is in the set described by (ab)*.
questions.explain: Strings in (ab)* repeat ab (ab, abab, ...). They never contain bb, and every nonempty one ends in b, while abba ends in a.

questions.q: A multiple-select question has 4 options, each worth 1 point under the instructor's grading. Two options are true and two are false. You select exactly one of the true options and nothing else. What percentage of the question's points do you get?
questions.explain: Each option is graded separately. You get credit for selecting a true option or leaving a false option unselected. Here you are right on 3 of 4 options (one true selected, two false left blank) and wrong on 1 (a true option missed), so 3/4 = 75%.

questions.q: A 4-point multiple-select question (1 point per option): options A and C are true, B and D are false. You select A, B, and D. How many points do you earn?
questions.explain: A: true and selected, +1. B: false but selected, 0. C: true but not selected, 0. D: false but selected, 0. Total = 1 point. Selecting a false option loses that option's point.

questions.q: On this instructor's multiple-select questions, 'choose none of the options' can be the correct answer.
questions.explain: At least one option is always correct, so selecting nothing is never the right answer. Canvas grades these differently, so the instructor or TA grades them by hand, one option at a time.

questions.q: For any regular expression u, what does ∅u (equivalently u∅) equal?
questions.explain: Concatenation takes one string from each set. If one set is empty, there is nothing to take, so no strings can be formed: ∅u = u∅ = ∅.

questions.q: What does ∅* equal?
choices: λ (the set containing only the empty string)
questions.explain: ∅* = ∅⁰ ∪ ∅¹ ∪ ∅² ∪ ... . ∅⁰ = {λ}, and every higher power is empty, so the union is {λ}. That is, ∅* = λ.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a valid regular expression identity?
questions.explain: Concatenation is not commutative, so order matters. Distributing from the right keeps w on the right: (u ∪ v)w = uw ∪ vw. The other three are real identities: left distribution, repetition doesn't matter, and starring twice adds nothing.

questions.q: Use identities to simplify ∅a ∪ λb.
questions.explain: ∅a = ∅ and λb = b, giving ∅ ∪ b. Swap the order to get b ∪ ∅, and u ∪ ∅ = u, so the result is b.

questions.q: Use identities to rewrite a(b ∪ λ) without parentheses.
questions.explain: Distribute from the left: a(b ∪ λ) = ab ∪ aλ, and aλ = a, so the result is ab ∪ a. The a stays on the left because concatenation order matters.

questions.q: Why is (u*)* = u*?
choices: Because u* is always a finite set
Any concatenation of strings from u* is already a string in u*, so starring again adds nothing new
Because the second star removes λ
questions.explain: Example from class: {a, b}* already contains every string over {a, b}. Gluing such strings together again only produces strings that are already there.

questions.q: In the identity list, u, v, and w can stand for any regular expressions, no matter how complicated, not just single symbols.
questions.explain: In the class proof, whole subexpressions like b*ab* were treated as a single u or v when an identity was applied.

Here the star covers the entire u = b, which sits inside a union, and an outer star covers the whole union. In that situation the inner star can be dropped: (u* ∪ v)* = (u ∪ v)*. This step was used in the class proof.

questions.q: (b*a ∪ b)* = (ba ∪ b)*, because a star inside a starred union can always be dropped.
questions.explain: The star in b*a covers only part of that term, not the whole term, so it can't be removed this way. For example, a is in the left side (b* = λ), but in (ba ∪ b)* every a is preceded by a b, so a is not in the right side.

questions.q: For all regular expressions u and v, uv = vu.
questions.explain: Concatenation order matters. For example, ab ≠ ba. Union is commutative (u ∪ v = v ∪ u), but concatenation is not.

questions.q: In proving (a ∪ b)* = (b*(a ∪ λ)b*)*, the first step applies u(v ∪ w) = uv ∪ uw to b*(a ∪ λ). What are u, v, and w?
choices: u = b*, v = a ∪ λ, w = b*
u = b*, v = a, w = λ
u = a, v = λ, w = b*
u = b*(a ∪ λ), v = b*, w = λ
questions.explain: u is the factor on the left (b*), and v and w are the two parts of the union (a and λ). This gives b*a ∪ b*λ.

questions.q: In the same proof, (b*a ∪ b*λ)b* becomes b*ab* ∪ b*λb*. Which identity justifies this step?
questions.explain: The trailing b* is distributed from the right, so w = b* stays on the right of each term.

questions.q: In the proof, b*λ is replaced by b*. Which identity allows this?
questions.explain: λu = uλ = u. Putting the empty string before or after something changes nothing.

questions.q: When proving two regular expressions are equal using identities, what approach did the instructor use and recommend?
choices: List a few strings from each side; if they match, the identity is proved
Start from the more complicated side and simplify it, naming each identity used, until it becomes the other side
Convert both sides to DFAs and compare their numbers of states
Write both sides in set notation and compare how many elements they have
questions.explain: Start with the more complicated side (the right-hand side in the class example) and work toward the simpler side. Name the identity used at each step and say what u, v, w are. Checking a few sample strings is not a proof.

questions.q: Applying identities to both sides in parallel until they reach the same expression is a valid way to prove an equality.
questions.explain: The instructor said you can also work on both sides and meet in the middle, and that this is still a proof.

questions.q: You should expect to write a full identity proof, like the long one done in class, on a test.
questions.explain: Full proofs like that one are for practice only. They would take the whole test. At most a small piece of one might appear. The instructor is posting 5 more practice proofs with solutions.

questions.q: The list of regular expression identities will be attached to the test.
questions.explain: The identity sheet (the book's identities plus the one the instructor added) is always attached, and it may be needed on the second test.

questions.q: In the online regex-equivalence tool shown in class (which uses | for union), how do you write a ∪ λ?
questions.explain: You leave the alternative after the vertical bar empty: (a|) means a or the empty string. It looks odd, but it avoids typing λ.

questions.q: You design a DFA in JFLAP for a regular expression you were given. How can you check that your machine is correct?
choices: Check that the number of states equals the length of the regular expression
Have JFLAP convert your DFA into a regular expression, then check it against the given one with the equivalence tool
Make every state final and see whether JFLAP accepts the regular expression
Compare JFLAP's regular expression to the given one by eye; any difference means the DFA is wrong
questions.explain: JFLAP can generate a regular expression from your DFA. It will usually look different from the original, so use the equivalence tool to check whether the two describe the same set.

questions.q: How many components are in the formal definition of a deterministic finite automaton (DFA)?
questions.explain: M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F): states, alphabet, transition function, initial state, and set of final states.

questions.q: In a DFA M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F), what is the type of the transition function δ?
questions.explain: δ takes a state and a symbol (a pair from the Cartesian product Q × Σ) and returns a state. For example, δ(25¢, quarter) = 50¢.

questions.q: A DFA is allowed to have no final states at all.
questions.explain: The only constraint is F ⊆ Q, and the empty set is a subset of every set, so F = ∅ is allowed. It seems strange, the same way an empty language does, but the definition permits it.

questions.q: A DFA is allowed to have every one of its states be a final state.
questions.explain: Every set is a subset of itself (Q ⊆ Q), so F = Q is allowed.

questions.q: Why is F = ∅ allowed in a DFA?
choices: Because the initial state automatically counts as final when F is empty
Because the only constraint on F is F ⊆ Q, and the empty set is a subset of every set
Because F must be the complement of {q0}
It isn't allowed; every DFA needs at least one final state
questions.explain: The definition requires only F ⊆ Q. Since ∅ ⊆ Q for any Q, a machine with no final states is still a valid DFA.

questions.q: A DFA has 3 states and alphabet {a, b}. How many transition arrows must its state diagram have (count self-loops as arrows)?
questions.explain: δ is a function on Q × Σ, so every state has exactly one outgoing arrow per symbol: 3 × 2 = 6.

questions.q: A DFA has 4 states and alphabet Σ = {0, 1, 2}. How many transitions does it have?
questions.explain: |Q| × |Σ| = 4 × 3 = 12. Each (state, symbol) pair has exactly one next state.

questions.q: A DFA can get stuck in a state where some input symbol has no transition defined.
questions.explain: δ is a function, so it gives an answer for every (state, symbol) pair. The machine always moves somewhere, possibly back to the same state, and never gets stuck.

questions.q: What does the definition require about the initial state q0?
choices: Exactly one state is the initial state, and q0 ∈ Q
Any number of states may be initial, as long as they are in F
The initial state must also be a final state
A DFA may omit the initial state if it has at least one final state
questions.explain: One state is special: the initial state q0, which belongs to Q. Without an initial state (no arrow tip in the diagram), the machine isn't a proper finite automaton.

questions.q: In a DFA state diagram, how are the initial state and the final states marked?
choices: Initial: double circle; final: an incoming arrow tip
Initial: an incoming arrow tip; final: double circle
Both are marked with double circles
questions.explain: The initial state has the tip of an arrow pointing into it. Final (accepting) states are drawn with a double circle.

questions.q: In a DFA, the states must be named q0, q1, q2, and so on.
questions.explain: State names are up to you. For example, the vending machine used $0, 25¢, 50¢, and so on. The book and JFLAP use q0, q1, q2, ..., so the course usually does too.

questions.q: For most of this course, DFAs are treated as language acceptors: each input string is accepted or rejected, and final states mean 'accept'.
questions.explain: The vending machine, where a final state means 'something happens', is a special example. The 'machine that does something' view returns only with Turing machines at the end of the course.

questions.q: What is the alphabet Σ of the vending machine DFA from class?
questions.explain: The machine only understands quarters and half-dollars. {$0, 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, $1 or more} is the set of states Q, not the alphabet. A small alphabet is fine; a digital computer really only understands {0, 1}.

questions.q: Vending machine: δ(25¢ deposited, half-dollar) = ?
questions.explain: 25¢ + 50¢ = 75¢, so the machine moves to the 75¢ deposited state.

questions.q: Vending machine: δ(50¢ deposited, half-dollar) = ?
questions.explain: 50¢ + 50¢ = $1.00, which reaches the '$1 or more' state, where the bottle is released.

questions.q: Vending machine: what are δ(75¢ deposited, quarter) and δ(75¢ deposited, half-dollar)?
questions.explain: 75¢ + 25¢ = $1.00 and 75¢ + 50¢ = $1.25. Both reach '$1 or more', because overpaying still lands in that state.

questions.q: The machine is in '$1 or more' (bottle released, counter reset to 0), and a quarter is deposited. Which state does it move to?
questions.explain: After the reset, the next coin counts from zero, so a quarter leads to 25¢ deposited. The machine never goes back into the $0 state itself.

questions.q: How many entries are in the full transition table for the vending machine DFA (5 states, 2 symbols)?
questions.explain: |Q| × |Σ| = 5 × 2 = 10. The table is a neater way to write ten separate lines like δ($0, quarter) = 25¢.

questions.q: In the vending machine, what does the double-circled state '$1 or more' represent?
choices: A bottle of water is released and the counter resets to 0
The machine rejects the coins and returns them
The machine halts permanently and accepts no more coins
Nothing special; it is simply the last state drawn
questions.explain: In this example, the final state means something happens there: the $1.25 bottle is released and the counter resets. Most machines later in the course are language acceptors instead.

questions.q: Why not make '$0 deposited' the final state and remove the '$1 or more' state?
choices: A DFA's initial state is never allowed to be final
The machine would release a bottle as soon as it was plugged in, and again every time it was unplugged and plugged back in
The machine would then have no final states, which is not allowed
The transition table would need more than 10 entries
questions.explain: The final state means 'release a bottle', so making the initial state final would give away free water at power-on. The definition does allow the initial state to be final (F can even equal Q). The reason is the machine's behavior, not a rule.

questions.q: If a test asks you to give a machine, you may give its formal description (the 5-tuple plus a transition table) instead of a state diagram.
questions.explain: Either form is accepted: the state diagram, or the formal description with a transition table. The instructor finds the formal version harder to read. A readable JFLAP screenshot or file is also fine.
